title: How Do Cats Purr? 25 Throat Twitches Every Second 🐱
description:
How do cats purr? Muscles in the voice box twitch about 25 times a second, snapping the glottis open and shut as the cat breathes in and out, and a 2023 study found pads in the vocal folds that may help make that low sound.

pinned_comment: When your cat purrs, is it usually happy or worried? Tell me what gives it away 👇
script: Your cat's purr is a twitch, twenty-five times a second. But how? Deep in the throat sits the voice box, with a tiny gap called the glottis. A signal from the brain makes the muscles around it twitch, snapping that gap open and shut. Air rushes in, and the gap chops it into bursts. Air flows out, and it chops it again. That's why a purr just keeps going. In twenty twenty-three, scientists found another clue: tiny pads inside the vocal folds, which may help a small cat hit such a low note. Bobcats and cheetahs purr too, but lions and tigers don't seem to. And a purr doesn't always mean happy. Cats also purr at the vet, or when they're hurt. So when yours starts twitching away, do you think it's happy, or worried?
key_facts: Purring comes from laryngeal muscles opening and closing the glottis, signalled by a neural oscillator (Mental Floss, Scientific American)
Commonly cited about 25 times a second; Scientific American gives 25-150 Hz, Vienna 20-30 Hz
Cats purr breathing in and out (Scientific American)
2023 Current Biology study (Herbst et al., Vienna) found pads in the vocal folds that may explain the low sound
Bobcats and cheetahs purr; lions and tigers don't seem to (Mental Floss)
Cats also purr under duress, such as at the vet or recovering from injury (Scientific American)
